findings.title: Backup code path skips the TOTP check and does not consume the used backup code
findings.body: When a backupCode is supplied, the handler validates it against the stored list but never removes the matched code. The code comment says 'we delete all stored backup codes at the end', but the final prisma.user.update only sets backupCodes to null when the 2FA disable succeeds. The disable path therefore accepts a backup code and still succeeds, which is intended, but the matching code is not invalidated if the update fails. More importantly, the backup-code branch runs whenever req.body.backupCode is truthy, so a request that also includes a valid-looking backupCode bypasses the TOTP requirement entirely; this is the intended lost-access flow, but nothing ties it to the login flow's rate limiting, so brute force against the 10 short hex codes is unthrottled on this endpoint.

findings.title: Used backup code is stored as null inside the JSON array and never removed, leaving null entries and a race window
findings.body: After a successful backup-code login, `backupCodes[index] = null` is written back as JSON. Subsequent lookups call indexOf on the array, so the used slot is null and cannot match, which is correct, but the array is never compacted and the update is a read-modify-write with no guard. Two concurrent logins with the same valid backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either writes, so one code can be used twice. The update should be conditional (compare-and-set on the stored ciphertext) or done in a transaction.

findings.title: Backup codes have only 40 bits of entropy and are stored in a rate-unlimited path
findings.body: Each backup code is 5 random bytes (10 hex chars, about 40 bits). Combined with the login path, which only applies the general checkRateLimitAndThrowError per email, this makes online guessing of a single code feasible for a motivated attacker over time, and it weakens the 2FA guarantee. Longer codes or a stronger rate limit on backup-code attempts would be expected.

findings.title: Setup overwrites backup codes and secret before 2FA is enabled, and never clears them on failed enable
findings.body: Setup writes new backupCodes and a new twoFactorSecret while twoFactorEnabled stays false. The backup codes are shown to the user only after the TOTP enable step, but the codes stored are the ones returned by this call. If the user abandons setup, the previous state is replaced anyway; this is acceptable, but the backup codes are also accepted at login only when twoFactorEnabled is true, so the display-before-enable ordering means users see codes that are not yet active. Verify the enable endpoint persists the same codes it displayed, since nothing in the diff shows the enable handler changed.

findings.title: backupCodes state typed as never[] and the download URL is never revoked on close
findings.body: useState([]) infers an untyped empty array, so backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode) and the render path rely on loose typing. Also the blob URL created in handleSetup is only revoked when a new setup starts; resetState and the close button do not revoke it, so the backup codes text remains in memory until the next setup.

findings.title: onEnable is only called on close, so the parent refreshes state only after the user dismisses backup codes
findings.body: Previously onEnable() fired right after the TOTP code was accepted. Now it fires only when the user clicks close on the backup codes screen. Closing the dialog via onOpenChange or the Dialog's X button skips onEnable and resetState, so the parent never learns 2FA was enabled and the modal's step is left on DisplayBackupCodes when reopened.

findings.title: Lost-access toggle is only reset on success, so switching modes keeps stale backup code input and errors
findings.body: The lost-access button calls resetForm(false) which clears backupCode and totpCode but the form is also used with a shared totpCode field. Toggling mode also does not reset the TwoFactor/BackupCode field registration, and on success the code only resets form values, not the mode, relying on setTwoFactorLostAccess(false) which is fine, but a failed attempt in backup mode leaves errorMessage from the previous mode visible until the next submit.

findings.title: Backup-code error codes are mapped in onSubmit but IncorrectBackupCode is not in errorMessages, and the login form reuses totpCode for the 2FA step
findings.body: Errors thrown from authorize surface as res.error values. The branch-based mapping works, but the login form still submits the TOTP input value as totpCode when in backup mode, and the backupCode field is only populated when the user is in lost-access mode. If the user switches back from lost access, methods.setValue('backupCode', '') is called but the stale totpCode is not cleared in that path, so a previously typed TOTP can be sent with a backup code, causing authorize to take the backup branch and ignore the code the user intended.

findings.title: JSON.parse and decrypt on user.backupCodes can throw an unhandled error for corrupt data
findings.body: symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse run without try/catch. Malformed or legacy ciphertext produces an unhandled exception that returns a 500 with no error code instead of MissingBackupCodes or IncorrectBackupCode, and the same unguarded parse exists in next-auth-options.ts authorize.

findings.title: Backup code login and backup code flows are not tested end to end
findings.body: The only new test covers download, copy and close on the setup screen. Nothing exercises logging in with a backup code via Lost access, a used code being rejected, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The PR description says the change was tested manually, but the TODO left in the file confirms the login path is untested.
